meta_desc: Step-by-step NCERT Class 12 Maths Exercise 7.3 solutions on integrating trigonometric identities, plus a free 8-question quiz to test your integration skills.

quiz.title: Class 12 Integration (Exercise 7.3) Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on integrating trigonometric functions the Exercise 7.3 way — half-angle for squares, product-to-sum, and identities like tan²x = sec²x − 1. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Class 12 Integration using trigonometric identities

questions.q: Which identity is used to integrate sin²x?
questions.explanation: The half-angle form sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2 turns the square into a term you can integrate directly. (1 + cos 2x)/2 is the identity for cos²x.
Write cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2. Integrating gives x/2 + (sin 2x)/4 + C.

questions.q: To integrate sin 3x cos x you first rewrite it as:
questions.explanation: Product-to-sum: sin A cos B = ½[sin(A+B) + sin(A−B)], so sin 3x cos x = ½(sin 4x + sin 2x).
Use tan²x = sec²x − 1. Then ∫(sec²x − 1) dx = tan x − x + C.

questions.q: The product 2 cos 3x cos x can be rewritten as:
questions.explanation: 2 cos A cos B = cos(A+B) + cos(A−B), so 2 cos 3x cos x = cos 4x + cos 2x.
Using sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2, integration gives x/2 − (sin 2x)/4 + C.

questions.q: Which identity converts cot²x for integration?
questions.explanation: cot²x = cosec²x − 1, so ∫ cot²x dx = −cot x − x + C.

questions.q: ∫ sin 2x cos 3x dx uses the product-to-sum form giving the integrand:
questions.explanation: sin A cos B = ½[sin(A+B) + sin(A−B)] with A = 2x, B = 3x gives ½[sin 5x + sin(−x)] = ½(sin 5x − sin x).

faq.q: What does NCERT Class 12 Exercise 7.3 cover?
faq.a: Exercise 7.3 is about integrating trigonometric functions using identities rather than substitution. You rewrite sin²x and cos²x with half-angle formulas, turn products like sin 3x cos x into sums, and use tan²x = sec²x − 1 before integrating.

faq.q: How do I integrate sin²x and cos²x?
faq.a: You cannot integrate the squares directly. Replace sin²x with (1 − cos 2x)/2 and cos²x with (1 + cos 2x)/2, then integrate each term. The cos 2x part integrates to (sin 2x)/2.

faq.q: Why do we convert products of sines and cosines into sums?
faq.a: A product such as sin 3x cos x has no direct antiderivative, but the product-to-sum identities turn it into a sum of single sine or cosine terms, and each of those integrates in one step.

faq.q: How is tan²x integrated in this exercise?
faq.a: Use the Pythagorean identity tan²x = sec²x − 1. Since ∫ sec²x dx = tan x, the whole integral becomes tan x − x + C. The same trick works for cot²x using cosec²x − 1.
